stages.narration: Your bass can sound enormous on headphones, and then lose a third of itself the moment somebody plays it through a phone, or a club rig, or the ceiling speakers in a shop. This lesson is about why that happens, how to measure exactly how much you are losing, and what to do about it. It is built and measured inside DAW Pro, and nothing in it is an opinion: every number was predicted from first principles before anything was rendered, then measured off the render, and both go on the screen together. One warning up front, because it is the honest thing to say. Most of what this lesson is about lives at the very bottom of the spectrum, and small speakers barely reproduce it. On a laptop you will see this much better than you will hear it, so the pictures are doing the work.

Start from the beginning, in case this is new. A stereo recording is two separate signals: one for the left speaker and one for the right. Summing to mono means adding those two signals together into a single one, and playing that out of everything. It is not rare, and it is not an edge case. A phone speaker is mono. A single Bluetooth speaker is mono. Most large club systems deliberately fold the low end to mono, because a bass note spread across two distant subwoofers is a mess. A shop or a cafe with speakers in the ceiling is usually mono. And a listener standing off to one side of a pair of speakers is hearing something close to it. So mono is not a fallback you can ignore. It is a normal, common way for your music to reach somebody.

Here is the part that surprises people. Adding two signals together does not always make them louder. If the two are identical, they add up and you get twice the level, which is what you would expect. But if one of them is delayed, even by a very small amount, then at some frequencies the peaks of one arrive at the same moment as the troughs of the other, and instead of adding they subtract. That is called phase cancellation. And because a delay affects every frequency differently, what it does across the whole spectrum is a repeating pattern of holes, which is called a comb filter, because a graph of it looks like the teeth of a comb. This matters far more for bass than for anything else, for one simple reason. Bass notes are long, slow waves. A single cycle of a low E takes about twelve milliseconds. So a delay of a few milliseconds is already a large fraction of a whole cycle down there, while up in the treble the same delay is many whole cycles and it averages out.

So here is the experiment, built in the app rather than described. One bass line: forty seven notes, eight bars, written by hand, nothing sampled and nothing generated. Two instrument tracks playing that identical part, one panned hard left and one panned hard right — you can see that on the mixer, pan left one hundred and pan right one hundred. There is no widening plug-in, no reverb, and no effect of any kind anywhere in the project. The only thing that changes between renders is that the notes on the right-hand track get moved a few milliseconds later. That is not an artificial trick, by the way. Nudging one copy of a part slightly late is exactly what a lot of stereo widening does underneath, and it is also what happens by accident whenever a doubled part is not perfectly in time.

Before any measurement, look at the mechanism itself, because this is much easier to see than to hear. In a moment you will see two waves. The blue one is the left channel and the violet one is the right, and the thick green line is their sum — what a mono speaker actually plays. At first the delay is zero, the two copies sit exactly on top of each other, and the sum is bigger than either one on its own. Then the right channel slides six milliseconds late, and you should watch the green line rather than the other two. The note being drawn is an E two, at eighty two hertz, and six milliseconds is almost exactly half of one of its cycles, so every peak now meets a trough. At the very end nothing changes except the note itself: the same six milliseconds on an E one, one octave lower, and most of the sum comes straight back. Underneath you are hearing the two renders, no offset first and six milliseconds late second.

There is a formula for this and it is short enough to say out loud. When you add a signal to a copy of itself delayed by some amount of time, every frequency gets multiplied by the cosine of pi, times the frequency, times the delay. What that means in practice is that there are particular frequencies where the multiplier is zero — where the sound is simply gone — and they repeat, evenly spaced, all the way up the spectrum. At a delay of six milliseconds, the first dead frequency is at eighty three hertz. The next is at two hundred and fifty. Then four hundred and seventeen, and so on. That first one is the problem, because an E two on a bass guitar is eighty two point four hertz. It is sitting almost exactly in the hole.

So let us listen to it. The same eight seconds twice, both summed to mono. The first has no offset at all. The second has the right-hand track six milliseconds late. Same notes, same instrument, same performance, same gain. And that last point is deliberate: these two are not loudness matched, because the difference in level is the entire lesson. One single gain was applied to both of them, so what you hear is the real relationship. On screen while it plays is the app's own mono safety meter, on the master strip. It reads plus one point zero zero when the two channels are identical, and it swings down into the red when they start to cancel each other.

This is what the summing actually did, measured across the whole spectrum. The bright line is one render divided by the other: the six millisecond mono fold, divided by the no offset mono fold. The dashed grey line behind it is the prediction from that formula, worked out before either file existed. They lie on top of each other, which is the point of doing it this way round. Now look at the shape, because the shape is the surprise. This is not a filter that turns the bass down. It is a row of very narrow notches. In between the notches, nothing at all is lost. That is what a comb filter is, and it is why the damage depends so completely on which note you happen to be playing at the time.

Which brings us to the part that is genuinely hard to hear, so here it is drawn instead. This chart is the level of the bass, between forty and one hundred and thirty hertz, across seven seconds of that same passage, measured off both renders. The pale line is the version with no offset. The red line is the six millisecond version. The shaded bars are not chosen by eye — they are every window in which the two versions differ by more than six decibels, worked out from the measurements themselves. A playhead sweeps across at real speed while you hear each version in turn, so when the playhead is inside a shaded bar, that is the moment to listen. And notice what the picture says: it is not that everything got quieter. Some notes are untouched and others fall off a cliff.

Here is the same thing note by note. Nine different notes, one single delay, and the fundamental of each one measured before and after the fold to mono. The dark bars are the predictions and the bright bars are the measurements, and they agree to about a tenth of a decibel across all nine of them. Now look at the two ends of the chart. C three, at a hundred and thirty one hertz, loses about two decibels, which is nothing. E two, at eighty two hertz, loses thirty five. Same track, same delay, same everything, and a thirty three decibel spread between the best case and the worst. And here is the part worth remembering. E one and E two are the same note, one octave apart. One of them is destroyed, and the other one comes through almost untouched.

It gets more interesting if you take that one bad note apart. A bass note is not a single frequency. It is a fundamental, plus a stack of harmonics above it at two times, three times, four times that frequency, and those harmonics are most of what a small speaker actually reproduces. So here is that E two, harmonic by harmonic. The odd numbered ones land in the notches and disappear: the third harmonic loses twenty six decibels and the fifth loses twenty one. The even numbered ones land exactly between the notches and do not move at all — the second harmonic came back at three hundredths of a decibel, which is nothing. So the note does not simply get quieter. It gets hollow. Every other piece of it has been removed, and that change of character is something you can hear on a small speaker even when the level change down at the fundamental is invisible to it.

Now the result that catches everybody out, including me. If six milliseconds is bad, then fifteen milliseconds ought to be worse. It is not. Fifteen is two and a half times the delay, and in the same band it does less than a quarter of the damage: three point four decibels lost, against almost fifteen at six milliseconds. The reason is that the notches move. Making the delay longer does not make the notches deeper, it packs them closer together, and all that matters is where they land relative to the notes you are actually playing. So the amount of harm a delay does is not a property of the delay. It is a property of the delay and the music together. Listen to the two of them against each other now: six milliseconds first, then fifteen. And a warning about this one in particular, because it would be easy to leave it out. Almost all of the difference between these two is below one hundred hertz. Measured above two hundred hertz, where a laptop speaker actually works, they are three tenths of a decibel apart, which is nothing at all — on a small speaker they will simply sound the same. On headphones they are about six decibels apart in the bass and the difference is obvious. So if this pair sounds identical to you, that is the measurement, not your ears.

Now let us be honest about how much of this you can hear right now, on whatever you happen to be listening on. In the sixty to one hundred and ten hertz band, the six millisecond version loses almost fifteen decibels, and fifteen decibels is enormous. But a laptop speaker is physically too small to move much air below about two hundred hertz. So measure only the part above two hundred hertz — roughly what a laptop actually puts into the room — and the same two files differ by three point two decibels. That is a real difference, and it is above the level people can reliably notice, but it is nothing like fifteen. So if you are on laptop speakers and those two versions sounded fairly similar, you were not imagining it, and there is nothing wrong with your ears or your speakers. Headphones or a proper monitor will show you the whole thing. The charts are here so that the lesson does not depend on which of those you have.

Two controls, because a measurement without a control is just a claim. The first one is the left channel. Across all three renders it measures minus thirty one point eight nine decibels in that band, identical to the second decimal place. Neither channel was ever touched, and neither was made quieter. Everything you have seen is purely what happens when the two are added together. The second control is the delay itself. It was applied by moving notes rather than by a plug-in, so it was measured back out of the finished audio by cross correlating the left channel against the right. It came back at exactly zero, six, and fifteen milliseconds. The experiment did the thing it says it did.

So what do you actually do about all of this. Three things. First, keep everything below roughly one hundred and twenty hertz centred and single: one source, in the middle, not doubled and not delayed. If you want a bass to feel wide, widen the harmonics above that and leave the fundamental alone, because the fundamental is the part that cancels. Second, be suspicious of any doubling of a low part at all — a second take, a copied track, a short delay, a chorus, a stereo widener. Anything that makes two versions of the same low note arrive at slightly different times is doing exactly what you have just watched. And third, check, rather than trusting it. The mono safety meter sits on the master strip, and summing your mix to mono for ten seconds before you call it finished costs nothing and tells you straight away.

Everything in this video was built and rendered in DAW Pro and measured off those renders, with the prediction written down first every time. The build script, the measurements and the charts are all reproducible. If you take one thing away, take this: widen the harmonics, and keep the fundamental single. Thanks for watching.

description:
A wide bass sounds enormous on headphones and loses a chunk of itself the moment anything sums it to mono — a club rig, a phone speaker, a shop ceiling. This measures exactly how much, and shows the mechanism rather than asserting it.

THE SETUP
One bass line, 47 notes, eight bars, written by hand. Two instrument tracks playing the identical part, hard left and hard right. No widener and no plug-in of any kind: the only change between renders is nudging one track a few milliseconds late, which is what most widening tricks do underneath.

FOLDED TO MONO, 60-110 Hz
· no offset: -31.89 dB (the baseline)
· 6 ms offset: -46.87 dB — 14.98 dB gone
· 15 ms offset: -35.33 dB — only 3.44 dB gone

PREDICTED, THEN MEASURED
Summing a signal with a copy of itself delayed by tau multiplies every frequency by |cos(pi f tau)|. At 6 ms that is a null at 83.3 Hz, 250 Hz, 416.7 Hz… Nine notes were predicted from that formula before anything was rendered and then measured off the render; they agree to about a tenth of a decibel. E2 at 82.41 Hz sits on the first null and loses 35.0 dB. E1 — the same note one octave down — loses 2.9 dB.

ONE NOTE, HARMONIC BY HARMONIC
E2's odd harmonics land in the notches: the 3rd loses 25.6 dB, the 5th 21.2 dB. The even ones land between them and move by 0.03 dB. The note does not get quieter, it gets hollow.

THE CONTROLS
The left channel measures -31.89 dB in all three renders, identical to the decimal. The offset itself was measured back out of the audio by cross-correlation: 0, 6 and 15 ms, exactly as asked.

HOW MUCH YOU CAN HEAR
Said plainly rather than assumed: above 200 Hz — roughly what a laptop speaker radiates — the same two files differ by 3.20 dB, not fifteen. Headphones or a real speaker show the whole thing. The charts are measured off the renders so the lesson does not depend on your speakers.

WHAT TO DO
Keep everything below roughly 120 Hz centred and single. Widen the harmonics, never the fundamental. Sum to mono and check before calling a mix done.

DISCLOSURE
The narration is a synthetic voice, generated locally. No music-generation model was used.
